newsitem.title: USA: Lucid feels a little sorrow leaving space.
newsitem.headline: Lucid feels a little sorrow leaving space.

text.p: Homeward bound astronaut Shannon Lucid admitted on Wednesday she would be "a little sad" to leave space after a record-breaking flight.
Lucid, getting ready to ride home aboard the shuttle Atlantis, is on the final leg of her six-month space mission.
"I feel a little sad but all of this has to come to an end," she told the Sci-Fi cable TV channel. "You have to go home sometime and I'm ready to go home."

Last week, Atlantis docked with Russia's orbiting Mir space station to collect Lucid and drop off her replacement John Blaha. The two craft remained locked together for five days while supplies and equipment were unloaded, the fifth time the space superpowers have met in orbit.

"A few years ago people were talking about space being the next battleground," said Frank Culbertson, who heads NASA's shuttle-Mir programme. "We are so far from that now that I hope it is never talked about again. Right now space is where we are doing the most significant, visible and successful cooperation between Russia and the United States."
NASA plans five more dockings with Mir through 1998, by which time construction of the international space station, led by the United States and Russia, should be under way.

U.S. space endurance champ Lucid and her shuttle crewmates spent their last full day in orbit preparing for Thursday morning's planned touchdown. The Atlantis crew flexed the shuttle's wing flaps and test fired its manuevering jets in readiness for the planned touchdown at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre at 8:13 a.m. (1213 GMT).

The loss of part of the shuttle's hydraulic system caused NASA to impose stricter weather requirements for the landing but officials said conditions look good in Florida and the backup landing strip at Edwards Air Force Base in California.

The shuttle will be met on the runway by a team of doctors, nurses and paramedics, ready, if necessary, to treat Lucid. Doctors said she could expect to feel weak and woozy after her long stay in weightlessness.

"There's a lot of muscles I haven't used in six months so it's just going to take a little time to get back used to using them," Lucid said. "I just think I'll be tired a little bit, but I'll rapidly be my normal self."
